content: Splinter hemorrhages are small areas of bleeding that occur beneath the fingernails or toenails. They appear as thin, red to reddish-brown lines of blood under the nails and run in the direction of nail growth. These hemorrhages are named splinter hemorrhages because they resemble a splinter lodged under the nail. Splinter hemorrhages can be caused by an infection of the heart valves, known as endocarditis. They may also result from damage to blood vessels due to inflammation of the blood vessels (vasculitis) or from tiny clots that injure the small capillaries (microemboli). Additionally, trauma or injury to the nail can lead to the development of splinter hemorrhages. It is important to contact your healthcare provider if you notice splinter hemorrhages and have not experienced any recent nail injury. It is worth noting that splinter hemorrhages often appear late in the course of endocarditis. In most cases, other symptoms of endocarditis, such as fever or general malaise, will prompt a visit to your healthcare provider before the splinter hemorrhages become evident. To diagnose the cause of splinter hemorrhages, your healthcare provider will perform a thorough examination and may ask questions about your medical history, such as: When did you first notice the splinter hemorrhages? Have you recently injured your nails? Do you have a history of endocarditis, or has your healthcare provider suspected endocarditis in your case? Are you experiencing other symptoms, such as fever, shortness of breath, muscle aches, or a general feeling of being unwell? The physical examination will likely focus on the heart and circulatory system. Laboratory tests may include blood cultures, a complete blood count (CBC), and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). Additional diagnostic tests may include a chest X-ray, an electrocardiogram (ECG), or an echocardiogram. After consulting with your healthcare provider, you may want to document the diagnosis of splinter hemorrhages in your personal medical records. There is no specific treatment for splinter hemorrhages themselves. Management typically involves addressing the underlying cause, such as following your healthcare provider's recommendations for treating endocarditis.
